confirmed.title: Each refinement round discards all subsolver work on prior disjuncts (pop/re-assert is quadratic and drops learned clauses)
confirmed.detail: lazyCheckStar (lines 536-558) now does pop(); push(); assertFormula(not(D_1 or ... or D_k)) every round that found new disjuncts. In cvc5 a user pop removes everything user-context-dependent above the popped level: the CNF clauses and SAT/theory state for the previous refined formula, and SolverEngine::pop() additionally calls d_smtSolver->getPreprocessor()->clearLearnedLiterals() (solver_engine.cpp:2249). So each round re-preprocesses and re-CNFs the entire cumulative disjunction from scratch: total preprocessing/clausification work over k rounds is O(k^2) in the number of disjuncts, versus O(k) for the old scheme which asserted only the new disjunct's negation each round and let the incremental subsolver retain all clauses and learned facts about previously covered regions. Only the base predicate (level-1) preprocessing is reused. This is the deliberate tradeoff stated in the new header comment (bounded live assertions / per-assertion caches), but be aware it can be a net pessimization when the number of refinement rounds is large, since the SAT solver re-derives the structure of all previous disjuncts on every round. Not a correctness bug.

verdict.reasoning:
Every load-bearing claim in the finding reproduces concretely from the code, and the behavior is introduced by this diff (HEAD never popped).

1. The new loop is as described. /home/mudathir/all/cvc5/mudathir/src/theory/arith/liastar/liastar_extension.cpp lines 536-558: when new disjuncts arrived, it folds them into the cumulative `sub.covered` OR, then does `if (sub.pushed) sub.engine->pop(); sub.engine->push(); sub.engine->assertFormula(sub.covered.notNode());`. The old code at HEAD (verified via `git show HEAD:...`, lines ~533-543) asserted only `disjunct.notNode()` per new disjunct with no push/pop, so the subsolver retained all prior clauses and learned facts.

2. Pop really discards the prior round's work, exactly as claimed:
   - SolverEngine::pop() (src/smt/solver_engine.cpp:2242-2255) calls `d_smtSolver->getPreprocessor()->clearLearnedLiterals()` at exactly line 2249, as cited.
   - CnfStream's node-to-literal caches are context-dependent maps on the user context (src/prop/cnf_stream.cpp:41-42, constructed with `userContext` in src/prop/prop_engine.cpp:86-91), so the literal mappings for all disjuncts converted inside the popped frame are removed.
   - Minisat's user pop (src/prop/minisat/core/Solver.cc:1937-1987) calls `removeClausesAboveLevel` on both `clauses_persistent` and `clauses_removable` (lines 1972-1973); `clauses_removable` includes learned clauses, so learned clauses tied to the popped frame are physically deleted.

3. The quadratic asymptotics hold. In incremental mode, SmtDriverSingleCall::getNextAssertions (src/smt/smt_driver.cpp:204-215) feeds only assertions added since the last check (`d_assertionListIndex` is a CDO on the user context, restored on pop). Old scheme: each `not(D_i)` preprocessed/CNF-converted once, O(k) total over k rounds. New scheme: round k pops the frame containing `not(D_1 or ... or D_{k-1})` (erasing its CNF/SAT state) and asserts the brand-new node `not(D_1 or ... or D_k)` of size O(k) (lazyHilbert adds ~1 disjunct per round via getDisjunct/addCone), which must be fully re-preprocessed and re-clausified since the caches for its subterms were popped. Total O(k^2). Only the base predicate, asserted in getSubsolver (liastar_extension.cpp:507) before any push, survives pops, as the reviewer notes.

4. The subsolver is exercised every round: lazyHilbert -> LiaStarUtils::getDisjunct (src/theory/arith/liastar/liastar_utils.cpp:626-642) does checkSat + getValue, so the dropped SAT/preprocessing state is re-derived each round, not hypothetically.

Caveats consistent with the finding's own framing: it is a performance concern, not a correctness bug, and it is the deliberate tradeoff documented in the new Subsolver header comment (bounded live assertions vs. re-derivation). But the finding's specific technical content -- pop/re-assert makes total preprocessing/clausification work quadratic in the number of disjuncts, drops learned clauses and preprocessor learned literals every round, and only the base-level work is reused -- is accurate, newly introduced by this diff, and triggers on every run with more than one refinement round. So it is a real (performance) problem worth flagging, exactly as characterized.

confirmed.title: Each refinement round re-preprocesses the entire growing disjunction and discards all subsolver learning, making cumulative refinement cost quadratic
confirmed.detail: The new scheme in lazyCheckStar asserts a brand-new formula not(d_1 or ... or d_k) every round in a fresh frame. Although the live-assertion count is now constant (the stated rationale), the asserted node is new each round, so the subsolver must re-preprocess and re-clausify O(k) disjuncts on round k, giving O(k^2) cumulative preprocessing/CNF work over k rounds, versus O(k) total for the old one-assertFormula-per-new-disjunct scheme (where each not(d_i) was processed exactly once and stayed asserted). In addition, SolverEngine::pop() (src/smt/solver_engine.cpp:2242) clears the preprocessor's learned literals, and the user-context pop discards the SAT solver's clauses for the popped frame each round, so conflict clauses derived from not(covered) (which logically remain valid, since the new refined formula implies the old one) are relearned from scratch every round. For predicates with many convex cells this can be a significant slowdown relative to the committed baseline. This is a performance regression risk only, not a correctness bug; the refinement logic itself was verified equivalent (sub.covered folds exactly the nodes the old loop negated, with identical skolem substitution; the base predicate below the first user frame survives every pop; the skip case leaves the subsolver in exactly the {base, not(covered)} state lazyHilbert expects; multi-literal/shared-lambda and incremental main-solver push/pop scenarios produce correct sat/unsat answers in testing). A middle ground would be to keep the old per-disjunct assertions within the single pushed frame and only rebuild the frame when assertion count crosses a threshold.

verdict.reasoning: Every load-bearing claim reproduces concretely from the code. (1) The new lazyCheckStar (src/theory/arith/liastar/liastar_extension.cpp:537-559) does pop/push/assert of a brand-new node not(d_1 or ... or d_k) on every round that discovered new disjuncts, and the lazy loop runs one round per convex cell until complete, with addCone growing pairs each productive round — so the rebuild fires nearly every round and round k's formula has k disjuncts. (2) Quadratic re-preprocessing is real: SmtDriverSingleCall::getNextAssertions (src/smt/smt_driver.cpp:205-215) tracks already-processed assertions via d_assertionListIndex, a CDO in the user context, and the assertion list itself is a user-context CDList — SolverEngine::pop() rewinds both, so the next checkSat fully re-preprocesses the O(k)-sized refined formula; the old scheme (no push/pop, one assertFormula per new disjunct) preprocessed each not(d_i) exactly once, O(k) total vs O(k^2) cumulative. (3) CNF work is also redone: CnfStream's d_nodeToLiteralMap/d_literalToNodeMap/d_booleanVariables are context-dependent structures on the user context (src/prop/prop_engine.cpp:86-91, src/prop/cnf_stream.cpp:38-42), so the popped frame's Tseitin definitions for the disjunction are discarded each round, and Solver::pop destroys the frame's SAT variables via resizeVars. (4) SolverEngine::pop() at src/smt/solver_engine.cpp:2242 calls clearLearnedLiterals() (line 2249), exactly as the review cites. (5) MiniSat's Solver::pop (src/prop/minisat/core/Solver.cc:1937-1987) removes clauses above the new assertion level from both clauses_persistent and clauses_removable; learnt clauses are allocated at the max user level of their derivation (Solver.cc:1535), so conflict clauses derived from the frame's not(covered) clauses are deleted on every pop despite being logically implied by the next round's stronger formula. The problem is introduced by the diff (the baseline never pushed/popped the subsolver and never re-asserted old disjuncts) and is not hypothetical (many-cell predicates driving many rounds are the feature's target workload). The reviewer's framing is also accurate in its limits: it is a performance regression risk, not a correctness bug — the refinement logic, the skip-round state, and the base assertion surviving pops all check out. The only soft spot is magnitude (per-round checkSat may dominate the quadratic preprocessing term, and rewriter attribute caching amortizes some rewriting), but the review already hedges this appropriately ("risk", "can be a significant slowdown"), so the finding stands as a real, code-grounded trade-off the diff's rationale does not account for.
